title: Productive Congress or Executive Overreach? Capitol on Track for Fewest Bills in 50 Years
subtitle: Congress is on track to pass the fewest bills in 50 years while President Trump has signed over 240 executive orders, sparking debate over executive power and legislative dysfunction.

poll.question: Is Congress's low legislative output a problem?

options.label: Democratic Erosion

conservative.headline: Trump Gets Things Done With Executive Action While Dysfunctional Congress Drags Feet
conservative.byline: As seen on Fox News, PBS NewsHour, White House
paragraphs: While Congress sits paralyzed by dysfunction and partisan gridlock, President Trump is delivering results for the American people through decisive executive action—proving once again that bold leadership trumps legislative incompetence every time.

Republican lawmakers are openly acknowledging what voters already know: Trump is outperforming Congress by every measure. Representative Eric Burlison of Missouri gave a brutally honest assessment when he told Fox News, "I'd give Trump an A+. I'd give Congress a D." The contrast couldn't be starker—while the legislative branch dithers, the executive branch delivers.

Burlison doubled down on his criticism of congressional inaction, arguing that "Congress needs to reciprocate the kind of bold vision and courage that Trump has taken, particularly with DOGE." The Department of Government Efficiency has become a model for how aggressive reform can cut through bureaucratic red tape—exactly the kind of transformation that Congress refuses to pursue.

House Speaker Mike Johnson has made clear that Republicans understand Trump's executive actions are so popular and effective that they need to be made permanent. Speaking at the Conservative Political Action Conference, Johnson declared that "the president has over 300 executive actions already, and we are going to codify so much of what he's doing so that the next team can't unwind it." This is how you lock in transformative change for generations.

Conservative legal scholars argue that Trump is simply restoring the proper constitutional balance of executive power. John Yoo explained that Trump's actions are designed to "restore a pre-Watergate worldview" when the presidency had appropriate authority without constant congressional micromanagement and interference.

Republican Study Committee member Representative August Pfluger emphasized the urgency Republicans feel about translating Trump's executive agenda into permanent law, saying "What we really want to see is speed and aggressiveness" in moving these policies through Congress. The problem isn't Trump moving too fast—it's Congress moving too slow.

The legislative branch's historic incompetence has forced Trump to govern through executive action, but that's turned out to be a blessing in disguise. Without the chaos of congressional negotiation and compromise, Trump has been able to implement his America First agenda with unprecedented speed and efficiency. Congress can either catch up and make these reforms permanent, or continue to demonstrate its irrelevance.

President Trump didn't create congressional dysfunction—he simply refused to let it stop him from keeping his promises to the American people. While the swamp creatures in Congress argue about process, Trump focuses on results. That's the difference between leadership and legislative theater.

liberal.headline: Trump Bypasses Democracy as Congress Heads for Historic Low in Legislation Passed
liberal.byline: As seen on NBC News, TIME, MSNBC
paragraphs: American democracy is being systematically dismantled as Congress abdicates its constitutional responsibilities and President Trump seizes powers the founders explicitly gave to the legislative branch—all while Republicans in Congress stand silent, complicit, or cheering.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer warned that something unprecedented and dangerous is happening in Washington. Speaking to reporters in March, Schumer explained that while "the executive always wants to control more things," members of Congress have historically resisted presidential overreach regardless of party. But now, he said, "They just bowed down to the President, and they're surrendering their power." This is constitutional capitulation.

Democratic lawmakers are sounding the alarm that Congress must reclaim its Article I authority before it's too late. Representative John Mannion of New York declared at a Tuesday press conference that "now is the time for Congress to reassert the constitutional authority it continues to cede to the executive branch." But Republicans show no interest in defending their own institution's power.

Even former Republican congressman Fred Upton has admitted that the balance of power has collapsed. Reflecting on basic civics, Upton told MSNBC, "I learned ninth-grade civics: You've got three equal branches of government. But right now, the Congress is not one of them." When Republicans admit democracy isn't working, believe them.

Senator Gary Peters of Michigan released a comprehensive report documenting the administration's systematic assault on constitutional norms. The report details what Peters describes as "President Trump's lawlessness and campaign of intimidation" as the administration takes unprecedented action to sidestep constitutional constraints designed to prevent authoritarian consolidation of power.

The numbers tell a damning story of legislative collapse. NBC News reported that Congress is on track for the fewest bills passed in half a century while Trump has issued more executive orders than any modern president. This isn't efficient governance—it's the erosion of the separation of powers that protects us from tyranny.

What we're witnessing is not a disagreement about policy but a fundamental transformation of American government. Trump has demonstrated that if Congress won't give him what he wants, he'll simply take it. And congressional Republicans, far from defending their institution's prerogatives, are actively celebrating their own irrelevance. This is how democracies die—not with a bang, but with a whimper from legislators too cowardly to defend their own constitutional role.

History will judge this Congress harshly—not for what it passed, but for what it surrendered. The framers designed a system of checks and balances precisely to prevent the concentration of power we're now seeing. When Congress abdicates its duty, it doesn't just weaken itself—it betrays every American who depends on constitutional democracy for protection.

factcheck.headline: Separating Fact from Spin
paragraphs: Both sides are cherry-picking facts to support predetermined narratives about executive power. Here's what the data actually shows about congressional productivity and presidential action.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ Congressional output is at historic lows: NBC News confirmed that Congress has only passed six bills in Trump's first 100 days—the fewest in seven decades. Data shows 38 bills were signed into law in 2025, the lowest first-year legislative output since record-keeping began in 2010.

✓ Trump's executive orders have shattered records: Analysis by The American Presidency Project shows 243 executive orders signed by Trump so far this term—more than his entire first term and more than any president in a four-year period since Jimmy Carter.

✓ Trump has exercised congressional powers unilaterally: NBC News documented that Trump has acted alone on tariffs, war, and spending—all powers the Constitution explicitly assigns to Congress, not the president.

✓ Public confidence in checks and balances has collapsed: A PBS NewsHour/AP-NORC poll found that two-thirds of Americans say the system of checks and balances is not working well—a 12-point jump from one year ago and double the rate from December 2024 before Trump took office.
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: Trump's executive actions are legitimate responses to congressional dysfunction. Reality: While Congress is historically unproductive, the Constitution doesn't grant presidents extra powers when Congress moves slowly. Article I gives Congress—not the president—authority over spending, tariffs, and declarations of war. Frustration with legislative gridlock doesn't constitutional authority override.

✓ Fair Point: Congressional productivity genuinely is at historic lows, and both parties share blame for legislative paralysis. The criticism that Congress isn't fulfilling its basic lawmaking function is factually accurate.
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: This is unprecedented democratic backsliding unique to Trump. Reality: While Trump's executive order volume is record-breaking, previous presidents from both parties have expanded executive power when Congress was uncooperative. Obama issued executive actions on immigration after Congress refused to act; Bush expanded executive authority after 9/11. The trend toward executive power has been building for decades.

✓ Fair Point: The combination of record executive orders plus historically low legislative output does represent an unusual concentration of power. Trump exercising congressional authorities like tariffs and spending without legislative approval is constitutionally questionable regardless of which party does it.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

What both narratives miss is that this situation reflects systemic breakdown, not just one party's malfeasance. Congressional dysfunction has been worsening for decades as partisan polarization makes compromise nearly impossible. Presidents of both parties have responded by expanding executive authority. The judiciary has sometimes checked these overreaches but has also allowed significant executive expansion. This isn't a Trump problem or a Republican problem—it's a structural crisis in how American government functions.

The founders designed friction between branches as a feature, not a bug, to prevent hasty action and tyrannical power concentration. What we're seeing now is that system breaking down: Congress can't legislate effectively, so presidents act unilaterally, which further reduces congressional relevance, creating a vicious cycle. Whether you view Trump's actions as necessary leadership or dangerous overreach depends largely on whether you support his policy goals—but the constitutional question of whether presidents should exercise congressional powers unilaterally should transcend partisan preferences.

The Bottom Line: Congress is passing the fewest bills in 50 years while Trump has issued record executive orders and exercised powers the Constitution assigns to Congress. Both facts are true. Whether this represents efficient leadership or democratic erosion depends on whether you prioritize getting things done over maintaining separation of powers—a legitimate disagreement, but one that should be grounded in constitutional principles rather than partisan convenience.
